extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of propaganda/public_relations/political communication; practitioners of PR and rhetorical persuasion
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles and techniques for shaping mass opinion and managing crowds, including types of propaganda, sources of authority, delivery/rhetorical devices, and practical applications in politics, business, and entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sociological propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Aims to increase conformity with the environment that is of a collective nature by developing compliance with or defense of the established order through long term penetration and progressive adaptation by using all social currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This propaganda is 'the way of life' with which the individual is permeated and then expresses it involuntarily in film, writing, or art; it typically springs up spontaneously within a culture, reinforces the individual's way of life as best, creates an indisputable criterion for judgments of good and evil, does not directly result in action but prepares the ground for direct propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting opinion leaders / influencers
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and contract those who most influence public opinion (key experts, celebrities, existing supporters, interlacing groups, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bernays expedited persuasion by recruiting influential figures to seed the environment; using authoritative or prestigious intermediaries helps propagate messages through existing social channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority (ethos/credibility of the manipulator)
rubrics_metrics.description: The manipulator may be an orator, a group, a musician, an athlete, or some other person who moves a crowd to the point of agreement before calling for action; Aristotle believed ethos (credibility) contributes to persuasiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use figures or institutions whose perceived authority predisposes the crowd to accept the message; establishing or demonstrating credibility before making requests increases effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige (sources and maintenance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prestige is a form of 'domination exercised on our mind by an individual, a work, or an idea' that paralyses the critical faculty of the crowd and commands respect and awe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prestige can be 'acquired' (job title, uniform, judge's robe) or 'personal' (inner strength, success). Manipulators should avoid actions that call prestige into question and should maintain distance from the crowd so faults do not undermine prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery (visual, vocal, and verbal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The manipulator's ability to sway a crowd depends especially on visual, vocal, and verbal delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mastery of delivery includes rhetoric essentials (see Churchill's Scaffolding): correctness of diction; rhythm (long, rolling, sonorous sentences); accumulation of argument (rapid waves of sound and vivid pictures); analogy (link unknown to familiar); and 'wild extravagance' (expressions embodying the feelings of orator and audience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to the masses
rubrics_metrics.description: [Hitler's principle] Propaganda 'must be addressed always and exclusively to the masses', rather than to the 'scientifically trained intelligentsia.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shape messages for broad, popular receptivity; avoid tailoring complex, technical, or multi-faceted arguments intended for elites when aiming at mass persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target emotions rather than intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: [Hitler's principle] 'Propaganda must be aimed at the emotions and only to a very limited degree at the so‑called intellect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design messaging to evoke feeling (fear, pride, rage, sympathy) rather than rely on detailed logical argument when seeking to move large audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the message simple and few‑sided
rubrics_metrics.description: [Hitler's principle] 'It is a mistake to make propaganda many‑sided…The receptivity of the great masses is very limited…' — keep messaging simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confine communications to a few clear points that are easy to remember; avoid complexity that reduces uptake and retention among broad audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare the audience for worst‑case scenarios
rubrics_metrics.description: [Hitler's tactic] Prepare individuals (e.g., soldiers) for terrors of war so subsequent events confirm propagandists' prior statements and reinforce faith in government assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priming audiences to expect negative outcomes makes them more likely to interpret subsequent events as validating the message and increases acceptance of dire claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make no half statements — assert one right unflinchingly
rubrics_metrics.description: [Hitler's principle] Emphasize the one right which propaganda sets out to argue; do not present an objective study that includes enemy‑favoring truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present a single, uncompromising narrative in service of persuasion rather than balanced, ambivalent framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and persistence
rubrics_metrics.description: [Hitler/Le Bon principle] Confine propaganda to a few points and 'repeat them over and over.' Messages affirmed and repeated are often perceived as truth and spread by contagion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persistent repetition makes points feel truer; use repeated exposure across media and time to entrench messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation and example over argument (Le Bon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds are guided 'by examples not by arguments.' Imitation is a necessity for humans provided imitation is easy; influence requires that the example not be too far removed from the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use easily imitable models and visible behavior/examples to guide crowd beliefs and actions; avoid examples unattainable by the audience, which will nullify influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use in politics (applications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowd‑manipulation techniques are used across the political process — campaign rallies, town‑hall debates, declarations of war — to foster support for candidates and policies; public opinion polls provide approval ratings and identify wedge issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage events and polling data to time messages and select issues; adapt rhetorical and crowd techniques for electoral and policy mobilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial advertising: create an environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising serves as propaganda to prepare a future crowd; Bernays recommended selling the idea or environment (e.g., 'the idea of a music room') rather than merely product features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame products within desirable lifestyles or environments to make purchases emotionally and culturally attractive rather than focusing only on technical features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment crowd engagement techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Entertainment uses rhetorical techniques, polarizing personalities, and cues (chants, calls-and-responses) to excite crowds and boost participation and sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain high enthusiasm with lights, sounds, images, crowd participation; use polarizing figures and scripted cues to draw out emotions and collective responses; performers must be aware of and responsive to crowd mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flash mobs and electronically organized gatherings
rubrics_metrics.description: Flash mobs — gatherings organized in advance through electronic means that perform a specific action then disperse — can surprise, awe, or disrupt; they may be used as a tool of political warfare (mass walkouts, disrupt rallies, reorganize crowds after dispersal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizers can leverage social networks and mobile devices to coordinate large, synchronized crowd actions quickly; such events can serve both benign entertainment and deliberate disruptive or political purposes.
